Swallowed a button battery or magnet: If you suspect a button battery or more than one magnet was swallowed, go to A&E or call 112 immediately, even without symptoms. A battery can cause a serious burn in the food pipe within 2 hours.
Take the child to the nearest A&E right away; bring the battery packaging or a similar one.
If older than 12 months and swallowed less than 12 hours ago, on the advice of a doctor or 112, 2 teaspoons of honey can be given every 10 minutes on the way (up to 6 times).
Note the time it was swallowed.
Make sure battery covers on remotes, scales, toys and greeting cards are screwed shut.
Don't try to make them vomit.
Don't give honey to a baby under 12 months.
Don't wait just because there are no symptoms.
Drowning
If a child pulled from water doesn't respond or isn't breathing normally, call 112 immediately and start basic life support.
Get the child out of the water without putting yourself in danger.
If not responding and not breathing normally: start with 5 rescue breaths, then continue basic life support.
If breathing, lay them on their side, remove wet clothes, cover them and stay with them.
Even if they come round and seem well, always take the child to a doctor; breathing problems can develop hours later.
Don't press on the stomach to get water out.
Never leave a young child alone in the bath or by a pool, even for a few seconds.
Cuts and bleeding
If bleeding doesn't stop with 10 minutes of steady pressure, is spurting, or the wound is deep, wide or on the face, call 112 or go to A&E.
Wash your hands or wear gloves.
Press on the wound with a clean cloth or gauze for 10 minutes without stopping.
If the cloth soaks through, don't lift it; put a new one on top and keep pressing.
Once bleeding stops, rinse a small wound under running water and cover with a clean plaster.
For animal bites or injuries from rusty or dirty objects, go to a health facility the same day (tetanus and infection assessment).
Don't put cotton wool, tobacco, coffee or similar on the wound.
Don't pull out an embedded object; apply pressure around it and go to A&E.
Chemical or foreign object in the eye
If a chemical such as a cleaning product or limescale remover gets in the eye, start rinsing right away and call 112 or 114. Go to A&E for an object stuck in the eye, loss of vision or severe pain.
For chemicals: rinse the eye immediately under lukewarm running water for at least 15 minutes, holding the eyelids open.
Let the water run from the nose side to the outer edge so it doesn't reach the other eye.
Bring the product's packaging with you.
For a small particle like dust or an eyelash: have them blink or rinse with clean water.
Don't rub the eye.
Don't try to remove an embedded object.
Don't use eye drops unless a doctor recommends them.
Suspected fracture, dislocation or sprain
If bone is showing, a limb is deformed, or you suspect a neck or back injury, call 112; otherwise take them to A&E.
Don't move the injured part; support it in the position you found it.
For an arm injury, support the arm in a sling across the tummy.
For swelling, apply something cold wrapped in a thin cloth for 15–20 minutes.
If you suspect a neck or back injury, don't move the child; keep the head straight and wait for 112.
Ask a doctor before giving painkillers or food and drink; surgery may be needed.
Don't try to put a broken bone back in place.
Don't put ice directly on the skin.
Electric shock
Call 112 immediately for loss of consciousness, not breathing, burns or palpitations. See a doctor after any electric shock, even if the child seems fine.
Switch off the fuse or unplug before touching.
If the power can't be cut, move the child away from the source with a non-conducting object such as dry wood.
If not responding and not breathing normally, start basic life support.
If there's a burn, cool it under cool running water for 20 minutes and cover with a clean, non-stick dressing.
Don't touch the child with bare hands before the power is cut.
Don't intervene on a wet floor.
Broken or knocked-out tooth
Go to A&E for mouth bleeding that won't stop, a jaw injury or signs of head injury. If a permanent tooth is knocked out, get to a dentist within 30–60 minutes.
Press on the bleeding in the mouth with clean gauze for 10 minutes.
Hold the knocked-out tooth by the crown (white part), not the root.
If a permanent tooth is dirty, rinse it briefly in milk; don't scrub or dry it.
Carry the tooth in a small container of milk and go to a dentist straight away.
If a baby tooth comes out, don't try to put it back; still show it to a dentist.
Don't wrap the tooth in a dry tissue.
Don't rub the root or wash it with soap.
